lessons.title: Transformers and the National Grid
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is electricity sent across the country at hundreds of thousands of volts when our homes use 230 V?
objectives: Describe how a transformer works
Use Vₚ ÷ Vₛ = nₚ ÷ nₛ and Vₚ × Iₚ = Vₛ × Iₛ
Explain why the National Grid uses high voltage transmission
successCriteria: All: state the parts of a transformer and that it needs a.c.
Most: use the turns-ratio equation
Some: explain energy losses in transmission lines using power equations
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: energy supply networks; Maths: ratios
lessons.smsc: Moral: using resources efficiently for the benefit of communities

keywords.def: a device that changes the voltage of an a.c. supply
has more turns on the secondary coil, so increases voltage
has fewer turns on the secondary coil, so decreases voltage
the network of cables and transformers that carries electricity across the UK

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the power of a device with 230 V and 5.0 A.
State why a transformer cannot use d.c.

teach.heading: How a transformer works
bullets: Primary coil and secondary coil on a soft iron core
a.c. in the primary makes a changing magnetic field in the core
The changing field induces a voltage in the secondary
d.c. does not work: the field does not change
teach.note: Draw the core as a closed loop of soft iron with two coils. Ask: why does a d.c. supply give no output? (The field is constant so there is no induction.) Remind pupils that transformers change voltage, not power.

model.problem: A transformer has 1000 turns on its primary coil and 50 turns on its secondary. The primary voltage is 230 V. Calculate the secondary voltage.
model.answer: Secondary voltage = 11.5 V

teach.heading: Power in an ideal transformer
bullets: No energy lost: power in = power out
Vₚ × Iₚ = Vₛ × Iₛ
Step up the voltage: the current is stepped down
Real transformers are 90% to 99% efficient
teach.note: Link to the conservation of energy. Ask: if the voltage goes up 20 times, what happens to the current? It falls by a factor of 20.

model.problem: An ideal transformer steps 230 V down to 11.5 V. The secondary current is 2.0 A. Calculate the primary current.
model.answer: Primary current = 0.10 A

teach.heading: The National Grid
bullets: Power stations generate at about 25 kV
Step-up transformers raise the voltage (up to 400 kV)
High voltage means low current for the same power
Low current: less heating in the cables, so less energy wasted
Step-down transformers near homes reduce the voltage to 230 V
teach.note: Use the power-loss calculation: P(loss) = I²R, derived from P = IV and V = IR (I × IR). Make the comparison explicit with the numbers in the model. Ask: why not just use thick cables? Cost and weight of copper.

model.problem: A power line delivers 100 kW. The cable resistance is 2.0 Ω. Compare the power lost as heat when transmitting at 1000 V and at 10 000 V.
steps: Ten times the voltage means 100 times less power lost
model.answer: Loss = 20 kW at 1000 V but only 200 W at 10 000 V

teach.heading: Check: step-up
bullets: Select the correct answer
teach.note: Option A reverses the coils. Option C ignores the effect on current.

check.q: A step-up transformer used in the National Grid...
options: has more turns on the primary than the secondary
increases the voltage and decreases the current
increases the voltage and the current
check.why: A step-up transformer has more turns on the secondary, so the voltage rises while the current falls, keeping power almost constant.

practice: A transformer has 200 turns on the primary and 800 on the secondary. The input is 12 V. Calculate the output voltage.
A 24 V to 6.0 V transformer has a primary current of 0.50 A. Calculate the secondary current (ideal transformer).
Explain why transformers do not work with d.c.
independent: Core: Explain why electricity is transmitted at high voltage.
Extend: A transformer has 500 turns on the primary and 25 on the secondary. Calculate the output when the input is 230 V, and the secondary current if the primary current is 0.20 A.
Stretch: A 5.0 MW supply is transmitted down a line of total resistance 4.0 Ω at 250 kV. Calculate the current and the percentage of power lost.
exit: State the turns-ratio equation.
State one reason for using step-down transformers near homes.
lessons.homework: Draw the National Grid flow diagram from power station to home and explain the voltage changes at each stage.
lessons.send: SEND: give a flow-diagram template for the National Grid with sentence starters. EAL: pre-teach primary, secondary, transmit. Stretch: explain why real transformers are not perfectly efficient (eddy currents, resistance).

lessons.title: Atomic structure, nuclear notation and isotopes
lessons.bigQuestion: What makes carbon-12 and carbon-14 the same element but different atoms?
objectives: Describe the structure of the atom and the properties of protons, neutrons and electrons
Use atomic number, mass number and nuclear notation
Define isotopes and compare their structure
successCriteria: All: label protons, neutrons and electrons
Most: work out numbers of each particle from nuclear notation
Some: compare isotopes and explain why they have the same chemical properties
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: atoms and the Periodic Table; History of science: developing the model of the atom
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the order found even at the smallest scales of creation

keywords.def: the number of protons in the nucleus (Z)
the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus (A)
atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
a proton or a neutron

starter: Bismillah. State the charge of a proton, a neutron and an electron.
Describe the particles in the nucleus.

teach.heading: Inside the atom
bullets: Tiny dense nucleus of protons and neutrons
Electrons orbit the nucleus
Relative charges: proton +1, neutron 0, electron -1
Relative masses: proton 1, neutron 1, electron about 1/1840
Atoms are neutral: protons = electrons
teach.note: Draw a nuclear atom. Stress the scale: an atom is about 10⁻¹⁰ m across, the nucleus around 10⁻¹⁵ m, so most of the atom is empty space. Link to the Rutherford scattering model if time allows. Atoms are neutral because the number of protons equals the number of electrons.

teach.heading: Nuclear notation
bullets: Written as ᴬ_Z X
A = mass number (protons + neutrons)
Z = atomic number (protons)
Neutrons = A - Z
teach.note: Write ¹⁴₆C on the board and read it aloud: carbon with atomic number 6 and mass number 14. Check that pupils find neutrons as A − Z. The element symbol alone tells you Z, but is written for clarity.

model.problem: Carbon-14 is written ¹⁴₆C. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in a neutral atom.
model.answer: 6 protons, 8 neutrons, 6 electrons

teach.heading: Isotopes
bullets: Same number of protons, different numbers of neutrons
Same chemical properties (same electrons)
Different masses and sometimes different stability
Some isotopes are radioactive
teach.note: Compare carbon-12 and carbon-14 using a table. Ask: why do they react the same way? Because chemistry depends on the electrons. Nuclei with the wrong neutron-to-proton balance are unstable and decay.

teach.heading: Check: isotopes
bullets: Choose the best answer
teach.note: Option A confuses isotopes and ions. Option D is the common slip: mass number versus atomic number.

check.q: Which statement about isotopes of the same element is correct?
options: They have different numbers of protons
They have different numbers of neutrons
They have different numbers of electrons
check.why: Isotopes have the same atomic number (protons) but a different number of neutrons, and hence a different mass number.

practice: State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in ²³₁₁Na.
Uranium-235 and uranium-238 both have 92 protons. State the number of neutrons in each.
Explain why isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties.
independent: Core: Copy and complete: particle / relative charge / relative mass for protons, neutrons and electrons.
Extend: An ion has 17 protons, 18 neutrons and 18 electrons. Write its nuclear notation, mass number and charge.
Stretch: Explain why alpha particles in the Rutherford experiment were mostly undeflected but a few bounced back, linking to the structure of the atom.
exit: Define atomic number and mass number.
State the number of neutrons in ¹⁴₆C.
lessons.homework: Make a table of three elements with their protons, neutrons, electrons and symbols using nuclear notation, plus one isotope for each.
lessons.send: SEND: give a notation template with arrows pointing to A, Z, symbol. EAL: pre-teach nucleus, nucleon, isotope. Stretch: explain why nuclei with too many neutrons are unstable.

lessons.title: Alpha, beta and gamma radiation: properties, detection and background
lessons.bigQuestion: How can we tell which kind of radiation a source gives out, and where does background radiation come from?
objectives: Compare alpha, beta and gamma radiation: nature, ionisation and penetration
Describe how radiation is detected
Describe sources of background radiation
successCriteria: All: name the three types and their penetration
Most: identify radiation types from absorption data
Some: explain ionisation and background correction
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: radon and geology; Chemistry: ionisation
lessons.smsc: Moral: honesty and care when handling hazardous materials

keywords.def: removing electrons from atoms to make ions
how far radiation passes through a material
a detector that clicks or counts when radiation passes through
low-level radiation around us all the time

starter: Bismillah. State what the nucleus of an atom contains.
Name the EM wave with the highest frequency.

teach.heading: Three types of radiation
bullets: Alpha (α): a helium nucleus, 2 protons and 2 neutrons
Beta (β): a fast electron from the nucleus
Gamma (γ): electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus
Unstable nuclei emit radiation randomly
teach.note: Link the idea of radioactive decay to unstable nuclei, which cannot be predicted individually. Alpha is deflected least by magnetic and electric fields (it is heavy and positive); beta is deflected the other way; gamma is not deflected.

head: Type
Charge
Ionising
Stopped by
rows: paper or a few cm of air
thick lead or concrete reduces it

teach.heading: Detecting radiation
bullets: Geiger-Müller tube and counter: counts per second or minute
Photographic film: darkens when exposed
Count rate must be corrected for background
Net count = measured count - background
teach.note: Describe the GM tube: radiation ionises gas inside, causing a pulse that is counted. Film badges are used by workers. Pupils should know the correction by subtracting the background count measured with no source present.

model.problem: A student measures a background count of 20 counts/min. With a source and different absorbers, she records: no absorber 420; paper 415; 3 mm aluminium 160; thick lead 22. Which radiations does the source emit?
steps: Net counts: none 400; paper 395; aluminium 140; lead 2
Paper makes almost no difference: no alpha
Aluminium reduces the count a lot but not to zero: beta is blocked, something else remains
Lead reduces to about background: remaining radiation is gamma
model.answer: The source emits beta and gamma radiation

teach.heading: Background radiation
bullets: Radon gas from rocks (the largest natural source)
Cosmic rays from space
Rocks and soil, buildings
Food and drink
Medical sources and a small fraction from nuclear industry
teach.note: Show a pie chart. Emphasise that background varies with location (granite areas have more radon). Ask: how does a student correct experimental results for it? Many living things are exposed to a tiny dose throughout their lives; the issue is the higher dose from strong sources.

misconception.wrong: Background radiation comes mainly from nuclear power stations.
misconception.right: Most background radiation is natural: radon from rocks, cosmic rays, food and the ground. Nuclear power contributes only a tiny part.

teach.heading: Check: penetration
bullets: Choose the best answer
teach.note: Option B is a typical confusion between ionisation and penetration: the most ionising radiation is the least penetrating.

check.q: Which radiation is the most ionising but the least penetrating?
check.why: Alpha particles are large and highly charged, so they ionise strongly but are stopped by a sheet of paper or a few centimetres of air.

practice: State two differences between alpha and beta radiation.
Explain why a student must measure the background count before an experiment.
A source's count falls from 900 per minute to 300 when a thin metal sheet is inserted. Background is 30. What might the source be emitting?
independent: Core: Name three sources of natural background radiation.
Extend: Explain the process of ionisation and why alpha radiation is more ionising than gamma.

Stretch: A sample gives counts of 360 per minute with no absorber, 358 with paper, 355 with 3 mm aluminium and 150 with 5 cm of lead. The background is 40. Deduce the radiation emitted and justify it.
exit: State what gamma radiation is.
State what a GM tube detects.
lessons.homework: Draw a chart showing which absorber stops each type of radiation, and write a short caption explaining ionisation.
lessons.send: SEND: give a penetration diagram with the absorbers to label. EAL: pre-teach penetration, ionise, absorb. Stretch: explain deflection in electric and magnetic fields.

lessons.title: Nuclear equations: alpha and beta decay
lessons.bigQuestion: What happens to the nucleus when it emits an alpha or a beta particle?
objectives: Write and balance nuclear equations for alpha and beta decay
State the changes in mass number and atomic number
Identify the daughter nucleus
successCriteria: All: state that alpha decay changes mass number by 4 and atomic number by 2
Most: balance nuclear equations for alpha and beta decay
Some: complete a decay series with several steps
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: atomic structure; Maths: balancing sums

keywords.def: a nucleus emits a helium nucleus, ⁴₂He
a neutron changes into a proton and an electron is emitted
the new nucleus formed after decay
an equation that balances mass number and atomic number

starter: Bismillah. State the number of protons and neutrons in ²³⁸₉₂U.
Describe the nature of an alpha particle.
State the charge on a beta particle.

teach.heading: Balancing rules
bullets: Total mass number is the same on both sides
Total atomic number (charge) is the same on both sides
Alpha: A decreases by 4, Z decreases by 2
Beta: A unchanged, Z increases by 1
teach.note: Write the generic equations. In beta decay a neutron changes to a proton, so Z increases by one. The electron emitted is written ⁰₋₁e. Gamma emission changes neither A nor Z.

teach.heading: Alpha decay example
bullets: Radium-226 decays by alpha emission
Daughter: radon
Check the sums
teach.note: Pupils write down the A and Z of the parent, subtract those of the alpha particle, then use the Periodic Table to identify the element from Z. Check: total A before = after; total Z before = after.

model.problem: Radium-226 (²²⁶₈₈Ra) decays by emitting an alpha particle. Write the equation.
model.answer: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂He

teach.heading: Beta decay example
bullets: Carbon-14 decays by beta emission
Mass number stays at 14
Atomic number increases to 7: nitrogen
teach.note: Explain: a neutron changes into a proton and an electron; the electron leaves at high speed. Because the proton count rises by one, the element changes.

model.problem: Carbon-14 (¹⁴₆C) decays by beta emission. Write the equation.
model.answer: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e

teach.heading: Check: balancing
bullets: Select the missing nucleus
teach.note: Option A forgets to adjust Z; option D confuses alpha with beta. Ask pupils to show the sums.

check.q: ²³⁸₉₂U decays by alpha emission. The daughter nucleus is...
check.why: A: 238 - 4 = 234; Z: 92 - 2 = 90, so thorium-234. Beta decay would give neptunium.

practice: Write the equation for uranium-238 decaying by alpha emission.
Complete: ⁶⁰₂₇Co → ⁶⁰₂₈Ni + ?
Polonium-210 (Z = 84) emits an alpha particle. Write the daughter nucleus.

exit: State the changes in A and Z in alpha decay.
Complete: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ?

lessons.title: Activity and half-life
lessons.bigQuestion: Why can some radioactive materials be handled safely after days, while others stay dangerous for thousands of years?
objectives: Define activity and half-life
Calculate remaining activity or mass after several half-lives
Find half-life from tables and graphs
successCriteria: All: define half-life
Most: calculate activity after a number of half-lives
Some: find half-life from a decay curve, correcting for background
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: exponential decay and halving; Geology: dating rocks
lessons.smsc: Moral: responsibility for long-lived waste affecting future generations

keywords.def: the number of nuclei that decay each second, measured in becquerels (Bq)
one decay per second
the time for the activity (or number of unstable nuclei) to halve
cannot be predicted for an individual nucleus

teach.heading: Activity and randomness
bullets: Decay is random: we cannot say when a given nucleus decays
Activity: decays per second, in becquerels (Bq)
The activity falls over time as fewer nuclei remain
Half-life: time for the activity to halve
teach.note: Use a dice simulation: roll 100 dice, remove sixes, repeat. The numbers fall approximately exponentially. Stress random for each nucleus, but predictable for a large number. Half-life values range from fractions of a second to billions of years.

teach.heading: Half-life calculation
bullets: Number of half-lives = time ÷ half-life
Halve the activity that many times
Activity never reaches exactly zero
teach.note: Do the steps visibly. Typical pitfall: halving the time instead of the activity. Another: taking two half-lives as 'all gone'.

model.problem: A source has an activity of 800 Bq. Its half-life is 6.0 hours. Find its activity after 24 hours.
model.answer: Activity after 24 hours = 50 Bq

teach.heading: Finding half-life from data
bullets: Read the time for the activity to fall to half
Subtract background first
Check with a second half to be sure
teach.note: Use a graph with a decay curve. Show the method: draw lines from 640 to 320 and from 320 to 160; the time between each halving is the same. The count rates need background correction.

model.problem: The activity of a sample is 640 Bq at 0 min and 320 Bq at 15 min. Find its half-life and its activity at 45 min.
steps: Activity halves in 15 min, so half-life = 15 min
model.answer: Half-life = 15 min; activity at 45 min = 80 Bq

teach.heading: Check: half-life
bullets: Choose the best answer
teach.note: Option C confuses half-life with total decay time. Option D halves the half-life. Ask for justification.

check.q: A sample has a half-life of 10 days. What fraction of the unstable nuclei remain after 30 days?
check.why: 30 days is 3 half-lives, so (1/2)³ = 1/8 remain. It does not reach zero.

practice: A source has an initial activity of 1200 Bq and a half-life of 2.0 minutes. Find its activity after 8.0 minutes.
A sample's count rate falls from 480 per minute to 60 per minute in 18 hours. Find its half-life.
Explain why a source with a half-life of 5 seconds is no use for checking pipes underground.
independent: Core: Define half-life in your own words.
Extend: A measured count rate of 84/min includes a background of 4/min. After 20 minutes the measured count is 24/min. Find the half-life.
Stretch: A nuclear waste has half-life 30 years and activity 4000 Bq. How many years until it falls below 100 Bq? Give your answer to the nearest 10 years.
exit: State the unit of activity.
Calculate activity after 3 half-lives if it starts at 960 Bq.

keywords.def: exposure to radiation from a source outside the body; the object does not become radioactive
unwanted presence of radioactive atoms on or in an object or body
a radioactive isotope followed through a system to detect leaks or flow
treating cancer using radiation to kill tumour cells

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the activity of 480 Bq after 3 half-lives.
Name the three types of radiation.
State what ionisation does to cells.

teach.heading: Uses of radiation
bullets: Smoke detector: americium-241 emits alpha particles
Thickness monitoring: beta passes through paper or foil
Tracers: gamma emitters followed in the body or pipes
Sterilising: gamma kills bacteria on food and equipment
Radiotherapy: focused gamma beams destroy cancer cells
teach.note: Ask: why do we choose each type? Smoke detector: alpha ionises air, giving a small current that drops when smoke absorbs alpha. Medical tracers need short half-life so the patient has less exposure.

head: Use
Radiation and half-life
Reason
rows: ionises air; absorbed by smoke; safe in a sealed case
passes through paper, partly absorbed; count changes with thickness
penetrates and kills bacteria; the food does not become radioactive

teach.heading: Choosing the source
bullets: Match the radiation penetration to the task
Short half-life for the body; long half-life for monitoring
Sealed sources reduce contamination risk
teach.note: Use the model as a template for exam answers. A detail: for monitoring thickness, alpha would be completely stopped and gamma would hardly change, so beta is best.

model.problem: Explain why beta radiation is used to monitor the thickness of aluminium foil, but alpha and gamma are not.
steps: Alpha is stopped by even thin foil, so no change would be detected
Gamma passes through almost all of it, so thickness changes hardly alter the count
Beta is partly absorbed, so its count changes with thickness
Long half-life means the source needs little replacement
model.answer: Beta is the only radiation whose count changes noticeably with the foil thickness

teach.heading: Irradiation, contamination and safety
bullets: Irradiation: outside exposure; stops when the source is removed
Contamination: radioactive material on or in you; keeps irradiating
Alpha is most dangerous inside the body
Protection: tongs, lead shielding, distance, short time, sealed storage
teach.note: Radiation workers wear film badges and use gloves, tongs, shielding and distance. Stress that radiation dose affects health through damage to DNA, causing cancer, and high doses cause radiation sickness. Discuss benefits versus risks in medicine, which are carefully controlled.

misconception.wrong: A food that has been irradiated with gamma rays becomes radioactive.
misconception.right: Irradiated food is exposed to radiation but nothing radioactive is transferred, so it is not radioactive. Contamination would require radioactive atoms to get on or in the food.

teach.heading: Check: contamination
bullets: Choose the best answer
teach.note: Option A is the common mix-up. Option D confuses 'dangerous outside' and 'dangerous inside'.

check.q: Which statement describes contamination?
options: Radiation passes through a patient from an X-ray tube
Radioactive atoms get on the skin or are swallowed
A source is kept in a lead box
check.why: Contamination means radioactive material is on or in the body. Option A describes irradiation.

practice: Explain why a smoke detector contains an alpha source.
Give two precautions for someone handling a radioactive source.
Explain why a tracer injected into a patient should have a short half-life.
independent: Core: State the difference between irradiation and contamination.
Extend: A hospital uses a gamma source for sterilising instruments. Explain why gamma is used and why the instruments are not radioactive afterwards.
Stretch: Evaluate the use of radiotherapy for cancer, considering benefits, risks and how risks are reduced.
exit: Give one use of gamma radiation.
State why alpha is most dangerous when inside the body.
lessons.homework: Write a fact file on one use of radioactivity, covering radiation type, half-life, why it is suitable and safety precautions.
lessons.send: SEND: give a table with use / radiation / reason to match. EAL: pre-teach irradiate, contaminate, tracer. Stretch: explain the ALARA principle.

lessons.title: Nuclear fission and fusion
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a tiny amount of uranium release so much energy, and why is fusion so hard to achieve on Earth?
objectives: Describe nuclear fission and the chain reaction
Describe the parts of a fission reactor and their functions
Describe nuclear fusion and the conditions needed
successCriteria: All: state what fission and fusion are
Most: explain a chain reaction and the roles of the control rods and moderator
Some: compare fission and fusion and explain the conditions for fusion
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: energy changes; Geography: energy supply
lessons.smsc: Moral: weighing great benefit and great risk with responsibility

keywords.def: a large nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, releasing energy and neutrons
neutrons from fission cause further fissions
two small nuclei join to form a larger nucleus, releasing energy
material that slows neutrons so they can cause fission

starter: Bismillah. State the number of protons and neutrons in ²³⁵₉₂U.
State one advantage of nuclear power.

teach.heading: Fission and the chain reaction
bullets: A slow neutron hits a uranium-235 nucleus
The nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei and 2 or 3 neutrons
Energy is released as kinetic energy of the fragments
The new neutrons go on to cause more fissions: a chain reaction
teach.note: Draw the chain reaction as a tree of arrows. Unchecked, it is explosive: a nuclear weapon. In a reactor the rate is controlled. The energy comes from conversion of nuclear potential energy to kinetic energy and then thermal energy.

model.problem: Check this fission equation is balanced: ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + 3 ¹₀n.
model.answer: The equation is balanced for mass number and atomic number

teach.heading: Inside a nuclear reactor
bullets: Fuel rods: uranium-235 undergoes fission
Control rods (boron): absorb neutrons to control the rate
Moderator (water or graphite): slows neutrons
Coolant: carries thermal energy to make steam for the turbines
Thick concrete shielding absorbs radiation
teach.note: Draw the reactor core. Ask: what happens if the control rods are lowered? (More neutrons absorbed: slower reaction.) The moderator slows the neutrons because fast neutrons are less likely to cause fission. Emphasise the reactor produces heat, the rest is the same as a normal power station.

head: Part
Function
rows: absorb neutrons: raised or lowered to control the rate
slows neutrons so fission is more likely
removes the heat to make steam

teach.heading: Nuclear fusion
bullets: Two light nuclei join to make a heavier nucleus
Energy is released
Needs very high temperature and pressure to overcome repulsion of positive nuclei
Occurs in stars, including the Sun
teach.note: Link to Physics 8 stellar evolution. Fusion happens in the cores of stars because the temperature and pressure are huge (millions of degrees). On Earth, containing the very hot plasma is a challenge, which is why fusion power stations are still experimental.

right.title: Fusion
points: Needs very high temperature and pressure
Little long-lived waste but hard to achieve

teach.heading: Check: control rods
bullets: Choose the best answer
teach.note: Option C is a typical error: control rods do not slow neutrons; that is the moderator's job.

check.q: What is the job of the control rods in a nuclear reactor?
options: to absorb neutrons and control the reaction rate
check.why: Control rods absorb neutrons. Lowering them in decreases the rate of fission. The moderator slows neutrons; the coolant carries heat away.

practice: Explain what is meant by a chain reaction.
State two differences between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion.
Explain why a nuclear reactor has thick concrete walls.
independent: Core: Describe the function of the moderator and control rods.
Extend: Complete and balance: ²H + ³H → ⁴He + ¹n by checking mass numbers and atomic numbers (Z = 1 for each hydrogen isotope).
Stretch: Evaluate nuclear fission as the main source of electricity for a country, giving two advantages and two disadvantages and a conclusion.
exit: State what fusion is.
State why fusion needs very high temperature.

Some: calculate orbital speed and explain comet motion
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: satellites in weather and mapping; Maths: circumference

keywords.def: the curved path of one body around another due to gravity
an object that orbits a larger body, natural (Moon) or artificial
an icy body in a very elliptical orbit around the Sun
orbit above the equator with period 24 hours, so the satellite stays above one point

starter: Bismillah. Calculate the circumference of a circle of radius 5.0 m.
State what gravity does between two masses.

teach.heading: Gravity and orbits
bullets: Gravity provides the force that keeps a body in orbit
The body is always changing direction: its velocity is changing
Closer orbits: faster speed and shorter period
Planets: nearly circular orbits around the Sun
teach.note: The existing lessons already introduce gravity and the Solar System; this lesson extends to varied orbits. Use a ball on a string to show the need for a force towards the centre. Ask: what would happen if gravity switched off? (The body moves off in a straight line.)
cycle: Gravity pulls the satellite towards the planet
The satellite moves sideways at high speed
The path curves round the planet
The speed and radius must match to keep a stable orbit

teach.heading: Orbital speed
bullets: Speed = distance ÷ time
Orbital speed v = 2πr ÷ T
r from the centre of the body being orbited
T = time for one orbit in seconds
teach.note: Convert days or years into seconds with care. Link to the circumference 2πr. The result is average speed along the orbit.

model.problem: The Earth orbits the Sun at an average radius of 1.5 × 10¹¹ m in one year (3.15 × 10⁷ s). Calculate its orbital speed.
model.answer: Orbital speed ≈ 3.0 × 10⁴ m/s

teach.heading: Comets and elliptical orbits
bullets: Comets have very elliptical orbits
Fastest close to the Sun, slowest when far away
Gravity is stronger when near, so the comet speeds up
The tail forms as the Sun heats the ice and gas
teach.note: Draw the ellipse with the Sun at one focus. Halley's comet has a period of about 76 years. Ask: where has the comet the greatest kinetic energy? (Closest to the Sun.) Planets also have elliptical orbits, but they are almost circular.

misconception.wrong: A comet's tail trails behind it as it moves.
misconception.right: The tail always points away from the Sun, because it is blown away by the Sun's radiation and the solar wind, even when the comet moves towards the Sun.

teach.heading: Artificial satellites
bullets: Low polar orbit: period about 90 min, passes over poles; monitoring and mapping
Geostationary: 24 h period, above the equator; TV and communications
Geostationary orbits are far higher than low orbits
Higher orbit: slower speed and longer period
teach.note: Use the model to calculate the speed of a geostationary satellite. Remind pupils that all geostationary satellites orbit above the equator at the same height.

model.problem: A geostationary satellite orbits at a radius of 4.2 × 10⁷ m from the Earth's centre with a period of 24 hours (86 400 s). Calculate its orbital speed.
model.answer: Orbital speed ≈ 3.1 × 10³ m/s (about 3.1 km/s)

teach.heading: Check: orbit change
bullets: Choose the best answer
teach.note: Option A is the common idea that satellites are beyond gravity. Option C reverses the relationship.

check.q: Compared with a satellite in a low orbit, a satellite in a higher orbit has...
check.why: Higher orbits have weaker gravity, so the satellite moves more slowly and takes longer for one orbit.

practice: Calculate the orbital speed of the Moon, at 3.8 × 10⁸ m radius, with period 2.4 × 10⁶ s.
Explain why a geostationary satellite is useful for TV broadcasting.
Describe how the speed of a comet changes in its orbit and explain why.
independent: Core: Describe the difference between a low polar orbit and a geostationary orbit.
Extend: The ISS orbits at 6.8 × 10⁶ m from Earth's centre in 92 minutes. Calculate its speed in m/s.
Stretch: Explain why a satellite can't be geostationary above London.
exit: State the source of the force that keeps a planet in orbit.
State where a comet moves fastest.

objectives: Describe the scale of the universe and the order of stellar life cycles
Use an HR diagram and absolute magnitude to compare stars
Explain how red-shift and the cosmic microwave background are used as evidence for the Big Bang model
successCriteria: All: order the stages in the life cycle of a star
Most: explain how the evidence supports the Big Bang model
Some: write a developed six-mark explanation using evidence and reasoning
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: standard form and ratios; History of science: how models change with evidence
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflection on the vastness of the universe and the care taken in testing ideas against evidence

keywords.def: the distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m
a measure of the true brightness of a star, as it would appear from a standard distance
the stretching of light from distant galaxies towards longer wavelengths
microwave radiation arriving from all directions, the remnant of the early universe

starter: Bismillah. Name the two main fusion fuels in stars (hydrogen and helium).
State the order of colours of stars from hottest to coolest.
State the equation speed = distance ÷ time.

teach.heading: Scale of the universe
bullets: Solar System: the Sun and objects orbiting it
Galaxy: billions of stars held together by gravity
The Milky Way is about 100 000 light-years across
The universe contains billions of galaxies
teach.note: This consolidates Physics 8 content that earlier lessons cover. Do the light-year calculation: the light-year is a distance, not a time. The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away.

model.problem: Calculate the distance in metres of one light-year. (Speed of light 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s; 1 year = 3.15 × 10⁷ s.)
model.answer: 1 light-year ≈ 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m

teach.heading: Life cycles of stars
bullets: Nebula collapses under gravity to form a protostar
Main sequence: hydrogen fuses to helium for most of the star's life
Sun-like star: red giant, then white dwarf
Massive star: red supergiant, supernova, then neutron star or black hole
teach.note: Pupils should be able to state each sequence in order, give the cause of each change (fuel running out and balance of forces changing), and explain that heavier elements are made in stars and scattered by supernovae. Link to the HR diagram.

teach.heading: Reading the HR diagram
bullets: x-axis: surface temperature, hotter to the left
y-axis: absolute magnitude or luminosity; brighter to the top
Main sequence: a diagonal band
Red giants: top right; white dwarfs: bottom left
teach.note: Say that lower (more negative) absolute magnitude means brighter. Ask: a star is cool but very bright; where is it and what size? (Top right: red giant, very large.) Compare absolute magnitude (true brightness) with apparent brightness, which depends on distance.

teach.heading: Big Bang: the evidence
bullets: Model: universe began small, hot, dense about 13.8 billion years ago, and expands
Red-shift: light from distant galaxies is shifted to longer wavelengths
More distant galaxies show greater red-shift, so move away faster
CMB: microwave radiation from all directions, the cooled remnant of the early universe
teach.note: Teach this as the model the specification requires pupils to know and use, with its evidence. Do not editorialise. Evidence: red-shift tells us space is expanding; the CMB was predicted by the model and observed, which supports it. Ask: what would different observations have meant for the model?

model.problem: Explain how red-shift provides evidence for the Big Bang model.
steps: Light from distant galaxies has longer wavelengths than expected
Longer wavelength means the galaxies are moving away from us
Farther galaxies show greater red-shift, so they move away faster
Everything moving apart suggests the universe is expanding from a common starting point
model.answer: Red-shift shows the universe is expanding, which supports the Big Bang model

teach.heading: Check: the CMB
bullets: Choose the best answer
teach.note: Option C confuses red-shift and CMB. Option A is a typical statement but not a reason. Ask for the link between evidence and model.

check.q: Why does the cosmic microwave background support the Big Bang model?
options: It shows galaxies are moving apart
It is radiation from the hot early universe, stretched by expansion into microwaves
It proves the universe is infinite
check.why: The Big Bang model predicts radiation left over from the hot early universe, observed today as microwaves from all directions.

practice: Calculate the distance to a star 8.0 light-years away in metres.
State the order of the stages of a massive star's life cycle.
Describe how red-shift evidence shows the universe is expanding.
independent: Core: Complete a table of star types with temperature, brightness and HR position.
Extend: Explain why a red giant is brighter than the Sun even though its surface is cooler.

Stretch: Write a six-mark answer: 'Explain how the evidence from red-shift and the cosmic microwave background supports the Big Bang model.' Use at least two linked statements for each piece of evidence.
exit: State two pieces of evidence for the Big Bang model.
State what becomes of the Sun at the end of its life.

Explain why dry mass falls during germination
Explain why the seedling can photosynthesise later and become independent

Some: interpret a dry-mass graph and explain each stage

keywords.def: stored nutrients in a seed used for early growth
seed leaf that may store food or become the first leaves
the first root to emerge from a seed
the young shoot in a seed

starter: List the three conditions needed for germination.
Write the word equation for aerobic respiration.
Why does a plant need light?

teach.heading: What is inside a seed?
bullets: Embryo: radicle and plumule
Food store in cotyledons or endosperm
Stores: mainly starch, with lipid and protein
Tough coat protects the seed
teach.note: Different seeds store food in different places; peas store food in cotyledons while cereals use endosperm. Ask pupils to say why a seed needs a food store (no leaves yet).

head: Store
Used for
rows: Digested to sugar, used in respiration

teach.heading: From seed to seedling
bullets: Water swells the seed and activates enzymes
Enzymes digest starch to sugars
Sugars are respired for energy
Energy and materials build the radicle then plumule
teach.note: Link to enzymes: amylase digests starch to maltose, which is converted to glucose (name sugars generally). Respiration needs oxygen so waterlogged seeds can fail to germinate.
cycle: Sugars used for respiration and growth

teach.heading: Dry mass graph
bullets: Fresh mass rises as water is taken up
Dry mass falls at first
Reserves are used up in respiration
Dry mass rises once photosynthesis begins
teach.note: Fresh mass is misleading because of water. Dry mass means the seedling is dried to remove water. The lowest point is when the seedling starts photosynthesising enough to gain mass.

misconception.wrong: A germinating seedling gains dry mass straight away because it is growing
misconception.right: Early growth uses up the stored food, so dry mass falls until leaves photosynthesise

teach.heading: Model: interpret the data
bullets: Read the dip and recovery
teach.note: Show a sample data set (illustrative).

model.problem: Dry mass of 20 seedlings: day 0 = 5.0 g, day 4 = 4.2 g, day 8 = 3.8 g, day 12 = 4.6 g. Explain the pattern.
steps: Days 0 to 8: dry mass decreases by 1.2 g as the food store is respired to release energy
The seedling is growing but cannot photosynthesise enough yet
By day 12 the green leaves photosynthesise faster than respiration and dry mass rises
model.answer: Reserves are used until photosynthesis takes over, so dry mass falls and then increases

teach.heading: Check: using reserves
bullets: One answer
teach.note: The trap is chlorophyll in the seed from the start.

check.q: Why does a germinating seed not need light at first?
options: It uses stored food for energy and growth
It absorbs sugar from the soil
check.why: The seed has stored food reserves that are respired to release energy; it only needs light once leaves have formed.

practice: Name two food stores in seeds.
Why does dry mass fall in early germination?
Define radicle.
independent: Core: Describe the stages of germination using the cycle.

Stretch: Sketch and explain a dry mass graph from sowing to a mature seedling.

Name the first root.
What happens to dry mass first?

keywords.def: single-stranded nucleic acid that carries instructions for making proteins
base in RNA that pairs with adenine
three bases that code for one amino acid
a change in the DNA base sequence

starter: Name the four bases in DNA.

teach.heading: DNA and RNA compared (Higher/Paper 2 only)
bullets: DNA: two strands, double helix
RNA: one strand
Thymine in DNA, uracil in RNA
Pairs: A-T and C-G; in RNA A-U

points: mRNA carries the code to ribosomes

teach.heading: Model: copy DNA to mRNA
bullets: Match each base
Remember T is replaced by U in RNA
teach.note: Walk through the transcription step in one line, using the template strand.

model.problem: A DNA template strand reads TAC CCG AAA. Write the mRNA and the three codons.
steps: T pairs with A: T-A-C gives A-U-G
model.answer: mRNA: AUG GGC UUU (codons AUG, GGC, UUU)

teach.heading: A DNA change can change the protein
bullets: A base change alters a codon
May change one amino acid
Protein folds differently
Phenotype may change
teach.note: Example: sickle cell: one base change alters one amino acid in haemoglobin, giving a haemoglobin that distorts the red cell. Check your class set for the exact amino acid names if used.

teach.heading: When a mutation does nothing
bullets: Several codons can code for the same amino acid
A silent mutation has no effect
Many mutations occur in non-coding DNA
teach.note: The genetic code is degenerate. Use the model: GGC and GGA both code for glycine, while UUU (phenylalanine) to UUA (leucine) changes the protein. Compare the two cases.

teach.heading: Check: choose the effect
bullets: One answer

check.q: Which change is most likely to alter the phenotype?

A base change giving a codon for the same amino acid
A base change giving a codon for a different amino acid in an enzyme
check.why: A different amino acid can change protein shape and function. Non-coding changes and silent changes usually have no effect on the protein.

What is a codon?

How does a DNA change change a protein?
Define a mutation.

Some: predict probabilities of each phenotype

keywords.def: both alleles are expressed in the heterozygote phenotype
an alternative form of a gene
having two different alleles of a gene
the combination of alleles

teach.heading: Codominance (Higher/Paper 2 only)
bullets: Neither allele is dominant
Heterozygote shows both traits
Each allele is shown by a capital letter with a superscript
teach.note: Flag: Higher/Paper 2 only. In codominance neither allele masks the other. Roan cattle show both red and white hairs (not pink).

teach.heading: Human ABO blood groups
bullets: Alleles: I^A, I^B and i
I^A and I^B are codominant
Both are dominant to i
Genotype I^A I^B gives group AB
teach.note: Group A can be I^A I^A or I^A i; group B can be I^B I^B or I^B i; group O is ii. Use this for family examples.

teach.heading: Model: cross
bullets: Write parent genotypes
Draw a Punnett square
Count outcomes
teach.note: Take each gamete in turn and check each box.

model.problem: A parent with blood group A (I^A i) and a parent with group B (I^B i) have a child. Find the possible groups and probabilities.
steps: Gametes: I^A or i from one parent; I^B or i from the other
Offspring: I^A I^B, I^A i, I^B i, i i
model.answer: Each of AB, A, B and O has a probability of 1 in 4 (25 per cent)

teach.heading: Roan cattle
bullets: Red allele R, white allele W
RR red, WW white, RW roan
Roan has red and white hairs
teach.note: Contrast with blending: the red and white hairs are visible separately. Calves of two roan parents can be red, roan or white, in a 1:2:1 ratio.

misconception.wrong: Codominance means the alleles blend to make an in-between colour
misconception.right: In codominance both alleles are fully expressed, such as red and white hairs side by side

teach.heading: Check: heterozygote phenotype
bullets: One answer
teach.note: The trap is mixing up incomplete dominance and codominance.

check.q: A person has genotype I^A I^B. What is their blood group and why?

check.why: I^A and I^B are codominant so both are expressed, giving group AB.

final temperature minus initial temperature
energy needed to raise 1 g (or 1 kg) of a substance by 1 °C

teach.heading: Four types of calorimetry
bullets: Combustion: burn fuel to heat water in a metal can
Neutralisation: mix acid and alkali in a polystyrene cup
Displacement: zinc powder into copper sulfate solution
Dissolving: salt dissolved in water; measure change
teach.note: Compare the set-ups: neutralisation, displacement and dissolving use an insulated polystyrene cup with a lid, thermometer and stirrer. Combustion uses a spirit burner under a copper can of water. Ammonium nitrate dissolving is endothermic (temperature falls); neutralisation, displacement and combustion are exothermic (temperature rises). Safety: eye protection, alcohol burners, corrosive solutions.

head: Type
Apparatus
Measure
rows: temperature rise of water; mass of fuel burned

teach.heading: Calculating the energy transferred
bullets: Q = m c delta T
m: mass of water or solution in g
c = 4.2 J/g °C for water
delta T: temperature change in °C
teach.note: Take the density of dilute solutions as that of water, so 1 cm3 has mass 1 g. Divide Q by moles of limiting reagent to give energy per mole; convert J to kJ. Mark energy change as negative for exothermic reactions (enthalpy change). Use data given in the question for c.

model.problem: 25 cm3 of 2.0 mol/dm3 HCl is mixed with 25 cm3 of 2.0 mol/dm3 NaOH. The temperature rises by 13.6 °C. Calculate Q and the energy change per mole of water formed. (c = 4.2 J/g °C; 1 cm3 = 1 g)

teach.heading: Evaluating the results
bullets: Heat loss makes the measured rise too small
In combustion most energy escapes to the air
Incomplete combustion reduces the energy
Use a lid, a draught shield and a stirrer

misconception.right: Heat losses and the mass of water also matter. Energy released depends on the temperature change AND the mass of the solution, and heat loss makes the measured value too low.

Record the initial temperature for a few minutes
Add the second reagent and stir
Record the highest or lowest temperature

teach.note: Equation: CuSO4.5H2O (blue) reversible reaction CuSO4 (white) + 5H2O. Heating drives off the water (endothermic); adding water is exothermic and regenerates the blue colour. Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate is used as a test for water but does not show that water is pure. Do not heat the crystals above a gentle flame; the test tube should be held at an angle with the mouth pointing away.

The gases rise, cool and recombine
White solid forms again on the cooler upper part of the tube

teach.heading: Homologous series
bullets: Same functional group
Same general formula
Consecutive members differ by CH2
Similar chemical properties; physical properties change gradually
teach.note: Examples: alkanes CnH2n+2 (C-C single bonds), alkenes CnH2n (C=C), alcohols CnH2n+1OH (-OH), carboxylic acids CnH2n+1COOH (-COOH). Physical properties such as boiling point increase with the chain length. Ask pupils to give the formula of the next member after C3H8 (C4H10).

bullets: Determines how a compound reacts
All alkenes decolourise bromine water
All alcohols react with sodium
The rest of the molecule matters less

misconception.wrong: Isomers are the same molecule drawn in a different way.
misconception.right: Isomers are different compounds with the same molecular formula. They have different structures and often different properties. A different drawing of the same chain is not an isomer.

teach.heading: Isomers

teach.note: Reaction: hydrogen-2 (deuterium) + hydrogen-3 (tritium) gives helium-4 + a neutron + energy. Check the mass numbers: 2 + 3 = 4 + 1. Check the charge: 1 + 1 = 2 + 0. The mass of the products is very slightly smaller than the reactants; the difference is released as energy (E = mc squared is beyond this specification; do not require it).

teach.heading: The barrier: electrostatic repulsion
bullets: Nuclei contain protons: positive charge
Like charges repel
The repulsion grows as nuclei approach
Nuclei must get very close to fuse
teach.note: Analogy: pushing two like magnetic poles together. The nuclei must get very close before the strong nuclear force (very short range) takes over and binds them. Therefore the nuclei need a large amount of kinetic energy to overcome repulsion. Do not use the word 'bonds' for the nuclear force without explanation.

misconception.wrong: Fusion happens easily because nuclei are very small and attract each other.
misconception.right: Nuclei are positively charged and repel strongly. They must be given a lot of kinetic energy to get close enough to fuse.

teach.heading: High temperature and high pressure
bullets: High temperature: nuclei move very fast
Fast nuclei can overcome the repulsion
High pressure: nuclei close together
More frequent collisions give a higher fusion rate
teach.note: The Sun's core is about 15 million °C (approx.; verify), with the huge pressure from gravity. Fusion reactors on Earth need temperatures of roughly 100 million °C or more (approx.) and a magnetic field to confine the plasma, because no material container could survive. Short answer model: high temperature gives enough kinetic energy to overcome repulsion; high pressure brings nuclei close together so collisions are frequent.

model.problem: Explain why nuclear fusion needs a very high temperature and pressure.
steps: Nuclei are positively charged so they repel each other
High temperature gives nuclei enough kinetic energy to get close despite the repulsion
High pressure squeezes nuclei together so collisions are more frequent
So fusion is only possible in stars or specially built reactors
model.answer: High temperature overcomes electrostatic repulsion; high pressure increases collision rate.

teach.heading: Check: fusion
bullets: Whiteboards
teach.note: Option A is the typical confusion with fission. Option C reverses the effect of temperature.

check.q: Why do nuclei need a lot of kinetic energy to fuse?
options: to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between protons
check.why: Protons repel each other. The nuclei need enough kinetic energy to get close enough to fuse.

teach.heading: The hierarchy of the universe
bullets: Solar System: Sun and its orbiting bodies
Galaxy: billions of stars
Universe: billions of galaxies
The Milky Way is our spiral galaxy
teach.note: Use approximate figures with care: the Milky Way contains hundreds of billions of stars (approx. 100-400 billion; verify) and the observable universe has about two trillion galaxies in some estimates (verify). Say 'billions of galaxies' as in the specification. Distances: a light-year is about 9.5 x 10 to the power 15 m (verify). Our Sun is one ordinary star.

teach.heading: Units in astrophysics
bullets: Mass: kg; distance: m
Speed: m/s; acceleration: m/s2
Force: N; time: s
Gravitational field strength: N/kg
teach.note: N/kg and m/s2 are equivalent for gravitational acceleration. Typical values (approx.; use values given in the exam): Earth 9.8 N/kg, Moon 1.6 N/kg, Mars 3.7 N/kg, Jupiter about 25 N/kg.

Weight W = m g
g depends on the body's mass and radius
Weight is a force in newtons

check.q: An astronaut travels from Earth to the Moon. Which quantity stays the same?

lessons.bigQuestion: Will the Sun end with a bang or a whimper?
objectives: Describe the evolution of Sun-like stars from nebula to white dwarf
Describe the evolution of stars more massive than the Sun
Explain how mass decides a star's final stage

keywords.def: a cloud of dust and gas where stars form
long, stable stage where hydrogen fuses to helium in the core
large cool star after the core hydrogen is used up
explosion of a massive star at the end of its life

starter: Bismillah. State what force pulls a nebula together.
State what happens in the core of a main sequence star.

teach.heading: Sun-like stars
bullets: Nebula: a cloud of gas and dust
Protostar forms as gravity pulls the cloud together
Main sequence: hydrogen fuses into helium
Red giant, then white dwarf
teach.note: Sequence: nebula, protostar, main sequence, red giant, white dwarf. Gravity pulls inwards; heat and radiation pressure from fusion push outwards; main sequence is stable because they balance. When the hydrogen in the core is used up, the core contracts and the outer layers expand and cool (red giant). The outer layers drift off and the core remains as a hot dense white dwarf, which cools over time (approx. billions of years).

teach.heading: Massive stars
bullets: Same start: nebula, protostar, main sequence
Then expand to a red supergiant
Core collapses and a supernova explodes
Leaves a neutron star or black hole
teach.note: The spec points focus on the stages. Very massive stars create heavier elements by fusion, up to iron in the core, and the supernova spreads elements into space, which form new stars, planets and us. A neutron star is extremely dense; if the core is massive enough, a black hole forms (gravity so strong that not even light escapes).

teach.heading: Compare the paths
bullets: The mass of the star decides its fate
Both start with nebula, protostar, main sequence
Larger mass: shorter life on the main sequence
Heavier elements formed and spread in a supernova
teach.note: Ask: why do bigger stars live shorter lives? They use fuel much faster. Model answer below.

model.problem: Describe the differences between the life cycle of the Sun and a star much more massive than the Sun.
steps: Both begin as a nebula that collapses to a protostar and then a main sequence star
The Sun becomes a red giant; the massive star becomes a red supergiant
The Sun's outer layers drift away leaving a white dwarf
The massive star ends in a supernova leaving a neutron star or black hole
model.answer: Mass decides the end stage: white dwarf for Sun-like stars; neutron star or black hole for much more massive stars.

teach.heading: Check: end stages
bullets: Whiteboards
teach.note: Option A is the typical error of putting a black hole after any star. Option C is the wrong order.

check.q: Which is the final stage of a star like the Sun?
check.why: The Sun is not massive enough to become a supernova. It will end as a white dwarf.

teach.heading: The axes
bullets: Vertical axis: luminosity (Sun = 1)
Horizontal axis: surface temperature
Temperature decreases to the right
Hot blue stars on the left; cool red on the right
teach.note: Paper 2 only: separate Physics (4PH1) content. The unusual axis, with temperature decreasing from left to right, is a historic convention. Luminosity is often a log scale, with the Sun at 1. Typical temperatures: the Sun's surface is about 5800 K (approx.; verify); hot blue stars exceed 10 000 K. Colour: hot blue-white, then yellow, then orange and red.

teach.heading: Groups of stars
bullets: Main sequence: diagonal band, top left to bottom right
Red giants and supergiants: top right
White dwarfs: bottom left
The Sun is in the middle of the main sequence
teach.note: Draw a sketch on the board. Red giants are cool but very luminous, so they must be very large. White dwarfs are hot but dim, so they must be very small. Most stars (about 90%, approx.) are on the main sequence. Stars move on the diagram as they evolve: from the main sequence to red giant, and then to the white dwarf region.

Core shrinks and outer layers lost

keywords.def: the universe began from a hot, dense state and has been expanding since
stretching of light from a receding galaxy to longer wavelengths
microwave radiation arriving from all directions in space
the increase in distance between galaxies

starter: State where microwaves come in the electromagnetic spectrum.
State what the Doppler effect is.

teach.heading: The Big Bang model
bullets: The universe began very small, hot and dense
It has expanded and cooled over time
Time began about 13.8 billion years ago (approx.)
Space itself is expanding
teach.note: Paper 2 only: separate Physics (4PH1) content. Avoid saying it was an explosion into empty space: space itself expands. Ask pupils to draw dots on a balloon, inflate, and watch the dots move apart; there is no centre. The age is approximately 13.8 billion years (verify the value used by the board). Check before use: Time began about 13.8 billion years ago (approx.; verify)

timeline.label: Later
timeline.text: Matter clumps into stars and galaxies

teach.heading: Evidence 1: red-shift
bullets: Light from distant galaxies is red-shifted
Galaxies are moving away from us
More distant galaxies show greater red-shift
So the universe is expanding
teach.note: Link to the Doppler effect: waves from a receding source are stretched to longer wavelength. Extrapolating backwards in time, all matter was once together. Pupils must say 'more distant galaxies are moving away faster'. Do not imply that Earth is at the centre.

misconception.wrong: Red-shift shows that the Earth is at the centre of the universe.
misconception.right: Every distant galaxy sees others moving away, like dots on an inflating balloon. There is no centre.

teach.heading: Evidence 2: cosmic microwave background
bullets: Microwaves arrive from all directions
Very nearly uniform
Remnant of the hot early universe
Stretched to microwave wavelength by expansion
teach.note: The CMB is radiation released early in the universe's history. As space expanded the wavelength stretched from very short to the microwave region; today it corresponds to about 2.7 K (approx.; verify). The Big Bang predicted it before it was found. Competing steady-state theory could not explain it.

model.problem: Explain how red-shift and the CMB support the Big Bang theory.
steps: Red-shift: galaxies move away from us, so the universe is expanding
More distant galaxies move away faster, matching an expanding universe
Expansion backwards in time suggests a hot dense start
CMB: leftover radiation from the early hot universe, stretched to microwaves, seen from all directions
model.answer: Red-shift shows expansion and the CMB shows a hot early universe, both predicted by the Big Bang theory.

teach.heading: Check: evidence
bullets: Whiteboards
teach.note: Option A would be blue-shift. Option D is a common wrong claim.

check.q: Light from a distant galaxy has a longer wavelength than expected. This shows the galaxy is...
check.why: Longer wavelength (red-shift) means the source is moving away from the observer.

teach.heading: Evaluating the theory
bullets: Two independent lines of evidence
Predictions tested by observation
Theories change as new data arrives
Questions remain: what came before?
teach.note: Discuss science as an ongoing process: theory, prediction, observation. Ask: what would make scientists change their minds? Link to respect for evidence and humility about what we do not know.

Stretch: Evaluate how the CMB supports the Big Bang more strongly than red-shift alone.
exit: Name two pieces of evidence for the Big Bang.
State what red-shift shows.
